newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Winterthur set for big earnings rise.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Winterthur set for big earnings rise.

text.p: Insurer HIH Winterthur International Holdings Ltd said on Thursday that it had secured substantial premium growth in calendar 1997 and was set to deliver a sizeable increase in earnings for the year.

"Our strategic alliances, organic growth and acquisition strategies have not only immunised us from cyclical downturns in insurance markets, they have positioned us well ahead of the game," Winterthur Chief Executive Ray Williams said in a statement announcing their purchase of Colonial Mutual General Insurance Company.
"We have already locked away substantial premium growth in 1997 and, subject to investment markets, we are also set to deliver a sizeable increase in earnings," Williams said.
Winterthur said it expected the New Zealand acquisition to generate A$20 million in premium income in 1998 and A$30 million by 2000.
Winterthur said under the terms of the acquisition, a strategic alliance would be formed with the Colonial Group CMH.AX for the exclusive distribuition of general insurance products in New Zealand.
"This acquisition represents an ideal opportunity to diversify our New Zealand operations in a similar manner to the successful approach we have adopted in Australia in recent years," Williams said.

Winterthur said it currently wrote premium worth A$250 million through the distribution channels of Australian banks, credit unions and building societies and expected that to grow to A$400 million over the next two years.
Winterthur has a strategic alliance with Colonial in Australia. National Australia Bank Ltd began selling Wintethur home insurance from July 1 under another strategic alliance.
"We are now showing that our clear Australian leadership can be leveraged offshore," Willams said.
Winterthur did not say in its statement how much it paid for Colonial's New Zealand unit.
It said it was now the second largest general insurance underwriter in the Australian market after the mutual National Roads and Motorists Association (NRMA).

A Winterthur spokesman later said the New Zealand acquisition had written 1997 premium worth around NZ$18 million and Winterthur's forecast that premium would grow to A$30 million by 2000 was conservative.

He said the purchase price would not be disclosed as it was worth less than five percent of Winterthur's assets. Acquisition prices are expected to be declared if they are worth more than five percent of existing assets.
The acqusition would be funded from cash reserves, the spokesman said.
The New Zealand company had about 30 staff and had 100 franchised agents selling insurance on its behalf.
Winterthur would continue to look through Australasia and Asia for similar strategic alliances and acquisitions to expand the distribution channels for its products, he said.
Winterthur posted net profits of A$61.5 million in 1996 on sales of A$1.35 billion, up from A$48.2 million in 1995 on sales of A$934 million.
Winterthur's shares were up two cents at A$3.08 by 11.15 a.m. (0115 GMT).
